rules.land: every status, with its 100 m grade; the app hides what the land filter excludes
rules.text: Loose gravel beside water that you can park next to and dig: the analyzer's gravel bars and creek beds on a named river or creek, and gravel pits right beside one, within 150 m of a road a car can use, where at least one gravel-friendly stone's map is in its top 20%; every land status is listed with its grade. Ranked by the chance that a target stone is really in the gravel: reported finds within 3 km and finds upstream on the same river carry the weight, the stone map only nudges; then how well the river places the bar, its size and how close you can park. A bar ranks higher when the river cuts the stone's source rock upstream (the first bars below a source hold the most, before side rivers dilute it) and lower below a dam (the reservoir traps new gravel), unless a side creek feeds it. Each bar says where to stand: the upstream head is boulders, the tail sand; the light tough stones (agate, jasper, wood, quartz) sit in the pebble band of the middle and downstream half, the heavy ones (garnet, staurolite) at the head with the black sand. A few map picks per state (hot stone map, nothing reported) ride along as a test of the map. Not yet tested against trips.

spots.label: gravel bar
placement: Inside of a bend (32° turn): where the current slows and drops gravel, a point bar
461 m below where a side creek joins: fresh material comes in here (it drains 67% granite)
A big bar (~4,400 m²): plenty of gravel exposed at low water
expect: Most of the gravel: dark basalt cobbles (keep the ones with white-filled gas pockets) and speckled granite.

Far-travelled stones too, from the whole basin upstream: hard, well-rounded quartzite and other cobbles that do not match the local rock; agate, jasper and petrified wood ride a river this size a long way.
Zeolites (map top 14%): white radiating crystals in the gas pockets of basalt cobbles.
Garnet (map top 9%): dark red grains in the black sand at bar heads; a gold pan finds them.
Opal (reported nearby or upstream, map cool, source rock cut upstream): glassy or milky seams and bubbles in basalt chunks, soft enough for a knife to scratch.
Agate & jasper (map top 13%): waxy, translucent or banded chalcedony pebbles; backlight anything that glows.
Plus plenty of handsome banded or spotted river rock that is none of these; keep what you like.
